See the discussion of the verse in the commentary below.

f. The Hebrew syntax is quite labored here. Literally, the verse begins: “That day and unto you he will come.” The Greek reads “your cities will be leveled.” The word for your cities (ʿārêk) would look the same as “unto you” (ʿādêkā), except it would have a resh rather than a dalet. These two letters are quite similar in Hebrew and are often confused. Nevertheless, the LXX is probably translating loosely to make sense of the text. It has “cities” a second time later in the verse where it is unattested in MT.

g. The word used twice for Egypt in 7:12 appears only four times elsewhere (Isa 19:6; 37:25 [=2 Kgs 19:24]; Ezek 27:8). LXX may have correctly picked up on a double entendre here in that the same consonants (mṣwr) could be “from Tyre” or “Egypt.”

h. The consonantal form of māṣôr could mean “Egypt” or from Tyre. The LXX translates the second example as “from Tyre to the River,” but this does not require a different consonantal text. “From Tyre to the River” (i.e., the Euphrates) actually makes better sense than the repetition of Egypt, and only requires a different vowel in the consonantal text (miṣôr rather than māṣôr).

i. It is not clear whether this opening line of 7:15 concludes the preceding verse or opens the next line.

j. The LXX has opsesthe which has a second-person masculine plural subject (“you will see”) rather than MT (I will show him). BHQ correctly labels this variant as a loose translation, probably done for stylistic reasons. BHK and BHS emend the text, substituting a he for the aleph so that the text does not change speakers (“show us marvelous things”), but such an emendation has no textual support. The NRSV follows this suggestion. The translation follows MT as a divine response to the petition in 7:14–15a.

k. While quite different, the LXX (eis martyrion) translates as “unto a witness,” but the LXX is not reading a different text. It simply translates lʿd with different vowels. The LXX reads lʿd as ləʿēd (“unto a witness”) rather than lāʿad (“into perpetuity”).

l. The LXX translates idiomatically again, based on contextual parallelism. Since the next line references the casting of iniquity into the depths of the sea, the LXX translates the unusual verb subjugate (kbš) as “cause to sink” (katadysei).

Since the appearance of Hermann Gunkel’s influential article, a significant majority of critical scholars have treated Mic 7:8–20 as a postexilic addition to the book.51 For decades, this majority opinion acknowledged the thrust of Gunkel’s three main arguments: (1) this text was composed in the postexilic period; (2) the alternating speakers and the addressees of 7:8–20 are best explained by treating this passage as a prophetic liturgy; and (3) the passage was written independently of Micah, complicating the interpretation of the passage (esp. in identifying the enemy of 7:8–10). All three claims have been disputed in recent years, with several scholars now seeing a closer relationship between the liturgical composition and the book of Micah as a whole.52 Others have questioned whether the change of speakers occurs as frequently as the MT suggests, and reject the label of liturgy altogether, and seek to place it in the eighth century.53

The “liturgical” nature of the extended passage has more to do with the changing speakers that extend through this larger unit than it does with the connotation that the passage mirrors an actual worship setting. The combination of the speaker and addressee changes too frequently to be accidental:

7:8–10:

Lady Zion addresses an unnamed enemy, here interpreted as Lady Nineveh



7:11–13:

The prophet addresses Lady Zion



7:14–15a:

The prophet intercedes for the people to Yahweh



7:15b:

Yahweh responds to the prophet’s intercession



7:16–17:

The people respond to Yahweh’s response



7:18–20:

The prophet addresses the community while speaking to and about Yahweh



Each of the changes in speakers and addressees must be deduced from the context, since they contain no introductory notes to the reader, but crucial syntactical information allows one to infer these changes.





1. Lady Zion Addresses Lady Nineveh (7:8–10)


8 Only reading 7:8–10 in English gives rise to the temptation to assume that the I who speaks these verses simply continues the speech from 7:7, where the prophetic I affirms his confidence in Yahweh’s salvific intentions. If one reads the Hebrew text, however, treating these verses as the speech of the prophet becomes problematic when the speaker quotes the enemy’s speech back to her in 7:10: Where is Yahweh your [second-person feminine singular] God? With this question, the enemy addresses a feminine entity, which cannot be understood as the prophet speaking in 7:1–7.54 Since 7:8–10 coheres tightly, the first-person speech is directed to an unnamed enemy who is also addressed in second-person feminine singular. Hence, in these verses, one woman speaks to another woman, and the first speaker should be understood as Lady Zion.55

Having identified the speaker of 7:8–10 as Lady Zion, the rhetoric of these verses is easy enough to follow, though the identity of the enemy has generated no small number of suggestions. Micah 7:8 begins the speech of Lady Zion directed to a feminine entity who is ambiguously named my enemy. Because of the wide acceptance of the view that 7:8–20 constitutes a postexilic text, those who have presumed that 7:8–20 arose independently from its current location at the end of Micah have generally sought to identify the enemy based upon these assumptions. Both Babylon and Edom have thus been named as possible enemies in this postexilic context.56 If this text were created independently, however, it simply does not provide enough substantive detail to arrive at a persuasive conclusion. Such assumptions, however, require the question as to why this passage appears here at the end of Micah. As noted both with chapters 4–5 and with chapter 6, there are good reasons to suggest that the expansively edited material in chapters 4–7 reflects a hermeneutic in which the material should be read as a literary construction that anticipates the future from the perspective of an eighth-century prophet. This same hermeneutic can also explain 7:8–20.57 Consequently, when read as the personified city’s response to the siege of Sennacherib, as well as a response to the punishment anticipated in 6:1–7:7, the assumption of Assyria as the enemy in 7:8–10 makes sense contextually and materially.

Micah 7:8 expresses Lady Zion’s affirmation of confidence in Yahweh’s ability to address her plight. The verse assumes Zion’s current situation reflects some kind of distress (I have fallen; I dwell in darkness). Logically, this distress is the result of the enemy’s actions, and the affirmation of confidence in this verse essentially parallels the prophet’s affirmation in 7:7. In this respect, it makes more sense to understand 7:8–10 as Zion’s response to the punishment assumed in the prophetic complaint in 7:1–7 (esp. 7:1, 4b). This suggestion also accounts for the reason why Lady Zion speaks. The charges leveled against the people and the leaders in 6:1–7:7 clearly have Jerusalem in view, so it makes sense that personified Jerusalem addresses the situation.

9 Micah 7:9 also makes sense contextually as a response to the preceding trial speech and lament in 6:1–7:7. The speaker, Jerusalem personified, uses juridical language and accepts the verdict (I will bear the indignation of Yahweh). Further, Lady Zion’s speech includes a confession of sins, one of the typical elements found in complaints that was noticeably lacking in both the trial speech (6:1–16) and the prophet’s complaint (7:1–7). This confession of sin equates her sin with the cause of the punishment and suggests a lengthy punishment will ensue (until the time when he takes up my case and he executes my justice), or at least acknowledges the indeterminate length of her punishment. Yet, as with 7:8, Mic 7:9 ends by affirming her confidence in Yahweh’s future salvific acts. The indignation to which Zion refers summarizes the plight of Jerusalem and Judah from the end of the eighth through the seventh centuries BCE.

The history of Judah in the seventh century in the biblical narrative unfolds as a long degeneration of the relationship between the kingdom and Yahweh. To be sure, Jerusalem was delivered from the siege of Sennacherib, but it lost territory and autonomy as a consequence of continued Assyrian dominance of the region throughout most of the seventh century. While Judah maintained a Davidic king on the throne, it nevertheless became a vassal state to the king of Assyria and remained so until the reign of Josiah, who—for a time—was able to expand his territorial control in the wake of the decline of Assyrian influence. When the Babylonians destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE, the yoke of Assyrian oppression was broken. It would soon be replaced by Egypt and Babylon as they fought for control of the Levant. Pharaoh Neco killed Josiah in 609 BCE (2 Kgs 23:28–30). Josiah’s son Jehoahaz replaced him, but only briefly until Neco took him to Egypt and placed another of Josiah’s sons on the throne, Jehoiakim. In 605 BCE Babylon defeated Egypt at the Battle of Carchemish and forced Egypt to return inside its borders. Jehoiakim continued to rule in Jerusalem, but he revolted against Babylon in 598 BCE, causing Nebuchadnezzar to lay siege to Jerusalem. During the lengthy siege Jehoiakim died and was replaced by his son Jehoiachin, who promptly arranged a surrender to Babylon. Jehoiachin, along with much of the leadership of Judah, was taken into exile in Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar placed a new king, Zedekiah, on the throne. A decade later Zedekiah also revolted against Babylon, leading to the destruction of Jerusalem and further exile of its people in 587 BCE.

Lady Zion acknowledges that she will suffer indignation until such a point as Yahweh takes up her case again. At that point she anticipates a different outcome (my justice, his righteous act). With this affirmation she turns once again to a denunciation of her enemy, Lady Nineveh.

10 Lady Zion tells her enemy that she will see the day when Lady Zion’s own fate changes. Micah 7:10 provides several further pieces of evidence that Lady Nineveh is the enemy in this passage. First, Lady Zion addresses her enemy using second-person feminine singular language, and this feature fits the pattern of addressing cities, especially capital cities, in feminine forms.58 Second, this feminine entity is a place. Third, the phrase like mud in the street is used in Nahum to refer to the downfall of Assyria (3:14; note also the similar phrase “pile in the street” is used for Assyria’s downfall in Isa 10:6). Fourth, the fact that the enemy taunts Lady Zion about the presumed importance of Zion’s God fits well with the assumption of Assyria imposing its will upon Jerusalem in various ways. Finally, as a vaticinium ex eventu (“prophecy from the event”), the prediction that Jerusalem will live to see her enemy’s destruction makes good sense considering Assyrian power in the Levant had waned for over a decade before Nineveh’s overthrow in 612 BCE. This prediction also serves a didactic function in the Book of the Twelve, connecting the warning of Micah to the warning of Nahum. At the time of Nineveh’s destruction, Josiah’s reforms were about a decade old, during which time he had expanded his territory into the former Northern Kingdom region of Samaria (specifically, Bethel).59 Lady Zion anticipates being around to see the fall of Nineveh: My eyes will look upon her. Now she will become a trampled place. In a real sense, then, Mic 7:10 literarily anticipates the themes of the book of Nahum.60





2. The Prophet Addresses Lady Zion about Reprieve and Punishment (7:11–13)


11 Micah 7:11–13 coheres through speaker, addressee, and chronology. The speaker of this passage must be the prophet (see below). As indicated by the second-person feminine singular suffixes in 7:11–12, the speaker addresses Lady Zion. All three verses predict events in the future. Despite these stylistic elements pointing toward homogeneity, the content of the verses creates real difficulty, as typically interpreted, in understanding them as the work of a single hand. Micah 7:11 sounds very much like a promise of weal: building the walls of Zion and extending the space apportioned for it. By contrast, the only possible interpretation of 7:13 is as a prediction of judgment: desolation of the land because of its action. In between, 7:12 can be interpreted positively as a pronouncement of restoration of those in the diaspora, a position that reflects the majority opinion.61 Micah 7:12, however, can also be interpreted as a message of judgment: An enemy will attack from every direction. The idiom of the verb bôʾ with the preposition ʿad can mean come to or it can be used in military contexts to mean “come against.” This latter interpretation of the verse makes better sense than does the majority opinion of 7:12 as a continuation of the promise given that Mic 7:8–20 is not an independent liturgy, but rather a composition designed to be read as though taking place in the time of Hezekiah.

The specific nature of the promise in 7:11 deserves careful note. The verse addresses Lady Zion, the personified city who represents the city’s fate. The prophet must be the speaker because the speaker refers to activity that only Yahweh can do: “he will extend the allotted space.” The word ḥôq refers to something prescribed or delimited. Most commonly, this word appears as a plural when referring to the prescribed statutes that Israel must follow, but in this verse, the singular form must refer to something else.62 In this instance, the most likely meaning is the prescribed, or allotted, space that Yahweh has provided to something. The promise of 7:11, therefore, announces to Zion that she will have time to build walls and extend her allotted space. Such a promise certainly makes sense in the aftermath of the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE, and similar expressions of hope appear in Zech 1:16; 2:1–4 in conjunction with the rebuilding of the temple and the city.63 Yet, the promise can also be understood against the backdrop of the reign of Hezekiah, and in the larger context of 7:11–13 this setting makes sense of the three verses together. Lady Zion has already acknowledged to Lady Nineveh that she will bear the indignation of Yahweh (7:9). The astute reader of 7:8–20 hears echoes of the anti-Assyrian polemic of Isa 10 throughout the final chapter of Micah.64 The superscription of Mic 1:1 associates the prophet with three kings, but Hezekiah undoubtedly plays the dominant role in the book. Certainly, the citation of the pronouncement of judgment from Mic 3:12 in Jer 26:12 assumes that Micah spoke those words during the reign of Hezekiah. As will also become clear, the ambiguity of 7:12 stems from a double entendre whose literary function becomes clearest when read against the backdrop of the events precipitating the siege of Sennacherib. Clearly, Hezekiah anticipated the possibility of Assyrian reprisal. In the biblical tradition, Hezekiah receives credit for building the tunnel that provided a source of water without having to go beyond the city walls.65 Just as significantly, however, Hezekiah also receives credit for extending the area within the walled city by building a second wall.66

12 Micah 7:12 can be read in two ways, as a promise or as a threat. The majority of commentators treat this verse as a promise for a return of exiled populations.67 When read as a continuation of 7:11, this verse makes sense as a promise to Zion to restore her population. In this scenario, the “he” who will come refers to an individuated member of the diaspora population, with the individual representing the whole. The you addressed in this verse is still the second-person feminine singular, and thus Lady Zion. In this light, the promise envisions a return from every direction: Assyria lies north and east; Egypt lies to the south; Tyre (if intended, see text note) sits on the Mediterranean coast north and west of Judah; the River refers to the Euphrates to the east; from sea to sea denotes the distant boundaries of the known world, or perhaps the ideal boundary of Israel to the east and the west; and mountain to mountain does the same for north and south. Further, if one assumes Mic 7:8–20 arose independently of the book as part of a worship liturgy for the postexilic community, then such an interpretation has much to offer. The problem with this interpretation, however, lies in the fact that it offers no explanation for 7:13 and the utter desolation it describes.

When one reads 7:12 closely, however, the lack of clarity regarding the identity of he means that one must determine the motivation for this journey. The particular phrase come to (bôʾ + ʿad in Hebrew) can be used in the context of a military attack.68 The meaning of the phrase thus depends upon who is coming and why. When one reads 7:12 with 7:13, the reason for the arrival becomes clear (at least for the final form of the text). He comes not in some glorious return, but he will come to bring desolation to the land. This he refers not to former exiles returning from the diaspora, but to foreign kings and their armies who come to attack Jerusalem.

13 Micah 7:13 unequivocally announces the future desolation of the land. For those interpreting 7:11–12 as an unadulterated promise, the jarring character of this verse poses problems. Consequently, many commentators ignore its interpretive significance or simply classify it as an isolated gloss.69 This rationale fails, however, to provide an adequate explanation of the verse’s content.70 A more satisfying interpretation of 7:13 comes from understanding 7:12 as a warning of the danger of foreign attack. The promise in 7:11 allows Lady Zion a reprieve, time to extend her walls before attacks from outside powers will come (7:12). The long-term effects of those attacks will result in desolation of the land (7:13a), and the rationale for sending this destruction rests with the consequences of the people’s actions (7:13b). The sequence of 7:11, 12, 13 poetically and prophetically describes what will happen to Jerusalem from the end of the eighth century to the beginning of the sixth century BCE. Jerusalem endures the siege of Sennacherib, but the autonomy of the Judean king becomes greatly restricted because the Assyrians destroy most of the cities in the Shephelah. Hezekiah’s successor, Manasseh, manages to stabilize the situation and rules for fifty-five years, though his political and religious accommodationist policies toward Assyria cause him to be condemned by the historian recounting the events of the seventh century BCE (2 Kgs 21). Manasseh’s grandson, Josiah, institutes theological and political reform that seeks to extend the power of Jerusalem’s monarch, but Egypt’s pharaoh kills him. Soon thereafter, Babylon defeats Egypt and gains control of the region, which leads to two unsuccessful rebellions by the Judean monarchs Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. The former was punished by the removal of a significant percentage of the leadership from Judah in 597, while the latter caused the destruction of the city and its temple in 587 BCE In the aftermath of that destruction, the surrounding kingdoms (including Tyre) took advantage of Judah’s weakened state and captured Judeans to sell as slaves. The postexilic author of 7:11–13 anticipates these events as though he were writing in the time of Micah. They describe long-term punishment, but not total annihilation for Zion and her people.





3. The Prophet’s Intercession and Yahweh’s Response (7:14–15)


The third subunit of 7:8–20 appears in the petition and response of 7:14–15. Whereas in the previous verses the prophet addressed Lady Zion with second-person feminine singular pronouns, the prophet petitions Yahweh in 7:14–15a using second-person masculine singular pronouns and verbs. A number of commentators emend 7:15b, but emendation hardly seems necessary if one can provide a satisfactory account for this statement.71 Treating 7:15b as Yahweh’s brief response to the prophet’s petition makes sense of the text as it stands.

14 Micah 7:14 begins with a second-person masculine singular imperative, spoken by the prophet to Yahweh on behalf of Yahweh’s people. The motive for the petition comes from the pronouncement in 7:13 regarding the desolation of the land for their actions. In this sense, 7:13 hardly seems like an outlier. The petition assumes the metaphor of Yahweh as shepherd and the people as the flock. The ambiguity of 7:12 returns in 7:14 with this metaphor. As previously noted, Mic 7:8–20 contains an inordinately high number of lexical clusters that evoke images from Isa 10. One of those connections comes with the use of the word staff (šēbeṭ). The word appears in Isa 10:5 in a divine speech in which Yahweh announces he will use Assyria as the rod of his anger to punish Yahweh’s people. The shepherd’s staff has both defensive and offensive purposes. To be sure, the shepherd may use the staff to ward off predators, but the shepherd also uses the staff to prod wayward sheep back onto the path where the shepherd would have them go. Upon the first reading of this petition, it is not immediately clear how the prophet intends Yahweh’s staff to be used: as a corrective rod or as a defensive weapon. This double entendre recedes quickly into the background with the remainder of 7:14–15a, which equates the action that the prophet desires with Yahweh’s act bringing the people out of Egypt. Nevertheless, the threat of Yahweh’s corrective action does not completely disappear, since reference to the exodus event centers around a forty-year wandering in the wilderness necessitated, according to the narrative account of Num 14, by the disobedience and fear of the people. Postexilic readers would have understood the parallel between the wilderness wanderings and the Babylonian exile.

15a The remainder of the petition offers an unusual scenario by describing the home of the flock with the terms Carmel, Bashan, and Gilead. Several things stand out about this unusual combination. First, all of these regions belong to the Northern Kingdom. Second, they all evoke connotations of lush, fertile land. Third, these regions all point to areas lost to Assyrian territorial expansions of the eighth century BCE.72 This understanding is articulated in Neh 9:32 where Ezra’s prayer petitions Yahweh to remove the punishment that has continued into the fifth century:

Now therefore, our God—the great and mighty and awesome God, keeping covenant and steadfast love—do not treat lightly all the hardship that has come upon us, upon our kings, our officials, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until today. (NRSV, emphasis added)

Too often, modern scholarship assumes that the return from exile represented a dramatic shift in terms of the people coming home. In reality, changes were gradual and uneven. Sometimes, expectations were high that the community was on the verge of dramatic change (see Hag 2:20–23; Zech 1:15–17), but other texts indicate that restoration efforts would take place on a much smaller scale than many had hoped (see Ezra 3:10–13).

15b Perhaps the most significant element in this unit appears in Mic 7:15b where, following the prophet’s intercession, Yahweh responds with a brief, yet powerful affirmation of his salvific intentions. I will show him signs. While a number of commentators and English versions opt to emend the text at this point due to the change of speaker, the rationale for doing so appears insufficient in light of the fact that changing speakers are characteristic of this text (which is why it is frequently called a prophetic liturgy).73 The word for signs refers often to miraculous deeds performed by God (e.g., Exod 3:20; 34:10; Josh 3:5; Jer 2:12; Pss 40:6; 72:18; 78:4; 86:10; 98:1; 106:22; 136:4; Job 5:9; 9:10).





4. The People Respond to Yahweh (7:16–17)


16 In Mic 7:16–17, the people’s speech responds to and interprets the divine response of 7:15b as judgment against the nations. Just as the nations showed great fear at Yahweh’s actions during the story of Israel’s taking of the land, so too will the nations cower in fear at the sight of Yahweh’s marvelous deeds here.74 The descriptions that follow in the remainder of 7:16–17 portray the nations with a number of images of terror and submission. First, the nations will see (Yahweh) and be ashamed of their own power, presumably because it pales in comparison to that of Yahweh. Next, the universal gesture of covering the mouth at the sight of something indicates great shock and fear. The statement that they will go deaf implies, perhaps, a loud sound accompanying the arrival of Yahweh.

17 The images of 7:17 portray the utter submission of the nations to Yahweh’s power. To crawl on the ground like snakes and serpents extends a typical metaphor that portrays submission to a powerful conqueror. Rather than merely bowing in obeisance or even licking the dust (see Ps 72:9; Isa 49:23), the nations will essentially slither to face their conqueror. Additionally, Yahweh will take the battle to them. Rather than Judah responding to a war of aggression, 7:17 assumes that the nations are in their strongholds when Yahweh comes to them. They do not offer resistance but throw themselves upon the mercy of Yahweh.





5. The People’s Hymn about Yahweh (7:18–20)


The final unit, 7:18–20, constitutes a hymn wherein the theme changes from the overpowering of the nations (7:16–17) to the forgiveness of the people (7:18–20). The people remain the speaker in 7:19–20, as indicated by the first-person plural suffixes. One should thus assume they speak in 7:18 as well. The unit is not independent, but functions as a continuation of 7:16–17. The unit speaks to and about Yahweh, but the vacillation need not be a sign of multiple hands. The rhetorical question that begins the unit represents a response to the promise of Yahweh’s divine response: Who is a God like you, forgiving iniquity and passing over rebellion for the remnant of his possession? The message that continues the rhetorical question artistically takes up the language of Exod 34:6–7, another case of prophetic intercession in the Pentateuch and a text that expresses Yahweh’s compassionate and just nature. The artistic character of this passage includes evidence of scribal contemplation combined with the use of allusions and word plays in this last unit. It was likely composed to conclude the book of Micah in the postexilic period.

In addition to the change of topic, these verses contain several allusions to other texts. At least three different foci for these allusions provide this subunit with a literary texture that brings the end of Micah into play with Exodus (specifically 34:6–7), Jonah (4:2), and the ancestral stories of Genesis. Micah 7:18 represents one of five texts that make use of Exod 34:6–7 in the Book of the Twelve (Joel 2:13; 4:21; Jonah 4:2; Mic 7:18–19; and Nah 1:3).75 Among these passages, Joel 2:13 and Mic 7:18–19 focus upon Yahweh’s compassion toward Yahweh’s people, while Joel 4:21 and Nah 1:3 emphasize Yahweh’s punishment of the guilty in Exod 34:7 and interpret the guilty as the nations who have taken advantage of Judah. Jonah 4:2 cites Yahweh’s predilection for mercy in Exod 34:6–7 as the reason why Jonah fled toward Tarshish. He could not bear the thought of Yahweh showing compassion to Assyria.

18 The artistic nature of the conclusion to Micah extends beyond the use of allusions. Micah 7:18 begins with paronomasia on the name of the prophet. The rhetorical question (Who is a God like you?) constitutes a word play on Micah (which means, “Who is like Yahweh?”). The question is answered in the remainder of Mic 7:18, since the allusions to Exod 34:6–7 evoke the first self-declaration of Yahweh about the character of Yahweh in the Old Testament and continue the exodus analogy of Mic 7:15b, 16–17. In Exod 34:6–7, Yahweh describes his own character as a God of inexhaustible compassion and ultimate justice. Micah 7:18–20 draws upon the vocabulary of Exod 34:6 to describe Yahweh’s compassion.

Mic 7:18–20

Exod 34:6–7



18Who is a God like you, forgiving iniquity and passing over rebellion for the remnant of his possession? He will not strengthen his anger forever, for he desires loving-kindness. 19He will again have compassion on us. He will subjugate our iniquities. And you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. 20And you will give truth to Jacob, loving-kindness to Abraham, that which you swore to our fathers from days of long ago.

6The LORD passed before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in loving-kindness and truth, 7keeping loving-kindness for the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and rebellion and sin, yet by no means clearing the guilty, but visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and the children’s children, to the third and the fourth generation.



The selection of Exod 34:6–7 is not random. This text represents the point in the Exodus narrative when Yahweh forgives and punishes the people after they have worshiped the golden calf. In the context of Micah, the parallels are clear. The prophet intercedes for the people (7:14–15a), and Yahweh responds (7:15b) with a promise of miraculous wonders, a word used most often in association with the liberation from Egypt. The fear of Yahweh’s power by the nations (7:16–17) also evokes exodus motifs. The allusion to Exod 34:6–7 highlights Yahweh’s compassion at the very point where the Israelites had reached their lowest—their abandonment of Yahweh to worship the golden calf while Moses was on Sinai. In the context of Micah, the last phrase of Mic 7:18 (he desires loving-kindness) echoes one of the three expectations of Yahweh articulated in Mic 6:8 (to love loving-kindness), helping 7:18–20 conclude Micah in the process. Functionally, these allusions underscore the compassionate character of Yahweh even while subtly reminding the people of Yahweh’s expectations of their own behavior.

19 The two halves of 7:19 reiterate the message of 7:18, but in two different ways: by continuing the allusion to Exod 34:6–7 and by evoking Jonah 2:3(4). Micah 7:19a continues the speech of the people and alludes to Exod 34:6–7, while Mic 7:19b cites the language of Jonah’s thanksgiving hymn. The two lines of 7:19a speak of Yahweh’s restoration of the people. He will execute compassion and subjugate the iniquity of the people. The affirmation that Yahweh will restore the people again does two things simultaneously. First, it reflects the people’s reaction to the response of Yahweh in 7:15b as a reversal of the current situation. For Yahweh to show compassion again implies that the current situation does not reflect Yahweh’s compassion. In this sense, the phrase shows that the people have experienced, or perhaps better, accepted Yahweh’s pronouncement of judgment in the book. Second, again underscores Yahweh’s compassionate nature because it implies he has exercised his compassion previously. This line of thought continues with the final verse of the book where 7:20 references Yahweh’s compassion to Abraham and Jacob in the days of long ago. Yahweh’s compassion to the ancestors of the people precedes their delivery from bondage in Egypt.

Micah 7:19b adds to the expression of Yahweh’s compassion by citing Jonah 2:3(4). A few commentators have classified portions of Mic 7:19 as secondary or see all of 7:18–20 as a late addition to the liturgy, but most of these arguments are too formalistic.76 At the same time, the location of 7:18–20 fits quite well as the hymnic conclusion to Micah.77 One suspicious element appears with the similarity of the language of Mic 7:19b to Jonah 2:3(4).78 In the broader context of the Book of the Twelve, the citation of Jonah 2:3(4) creates a link back to Jonah’s prayer and deliverance (2:2[3]) in the belly of the fish. This citation creates an analogy to what is happening in Mic 7:18–20 where the people respond to the deliverance announced by the prophet and Yahweh (7:16–17, 14–15 respectively). In all likelihood, this allusion was added to Mic 7:19 at the point that Jonah was incorporated into the Book of the Twelve.79 The focus on the punishment of the foreign nations in Mic 7:16–17 may have elicited this citation in Mic 7:19. Jonah portrays Yahweh’s compassion on foreigners, with Jonah 4:2 citing Exod 34:6–7 as proof of Yahweh’s compassion on the nations. Those tradents who added Jonah could well have been influenced by the theme of forgiveness and the connection with Exod 34:6–7 in Mic 7:18–20. They likely added this link back to Jonah’s profession of deliverance.80

20 As noted above, 7:18–19 draws upon other texts to undergird the message of Yahweh’s compassion. Micah 7:20 extends this allusive character to include two of the main characters from Genesis: Jacob and Abraham. Micah 7:20 cites these two ancestors in reverse order of their arrangement in the canonical traditions. Unlike the allusions in 7:18–19, the references to Jacob and Abraham do not appear to allude to specific texts. Rather, by evoking the names Jacob and Abraham, a unique pairing in the Old Testament, this allusion operates on two levels. First, it refers to the ancestor traditions in Genesis as a whole, with these stories repeatedly narrating episodes that emphasize Yahweh’s own faithfulness and loving-kindness. At every turn in these stories, Yahweh’s hand protects these characters. Second, Jacob and Abraham serve as a cipher for all of Yahweh’s people. The stories of Jacob center around Bethel and the central part of the Northern Kingdom while the Abraham stories generally have a more southern orientation. The covenant between Yahweh and Yahweh’s people began with Abraham as he three times receives the covenant promise of land, progeny, and blessing to the nations (Gen 12; 15; 17), but only with Jacob’s fathering of twelve sons does the threat to Abraham’s progeny recede.

In addition to the parallel of Jacob and Abraham, the gifts that Yahweh bestows to the people in Mic 7:20 also represent parallel concepts. Both ʾemet and ḥesed connote a sense of continuing fidelity. While some English translations (NASB, KJV, NKJV, CJB) translate ʾĕmet as “truth,” most use language related to faithfulness to avoid the connotation that this affirmation concerns dogma. The parallel usage of these two terms emphasizes their relational aspect; they portray consistent, true, kind, compassionate, and loving behavior. In this respect, the affirmation cuts two ways: as a reference to Yahweh’s ongoing fidelity and as a hope that Yahweh’s people will reciprocate. The allusions to the exodus and the ancestor narratives in the latter half of this chapter consistently evoke accounts of Yahweh’s compassion and fidelity toward Yahweh’s people. The prophetic confrontation of Yahweh’s people’s shortcomings throughout Micah has more than demonstrated their lack of ʾemet and ḥesed. Micah 7:8–20 assumes a people in desperate need of a reaffirmation of Yahweh’s continued benevolence. Yahweh has shown ʾemet and ḥesed, and 7:20 affirms he will continue to provide ʾemet and ḥesed to Jacob and Abraham’s descendants. At the same time, the verse pleads with Yahweh’s people to practice ʾemet and ḥesed, characteristics that have been in short supply for the people of Yahweh in Micah.

The final phrase of Micah (that which you swore to our ancestors from days of long ago) reiterates the long-standing relationship of Yahweh to Yahweh’s people, but it also causes the attentive reader to recall the specific recurring promise given by Yahweh to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This tradition of the promise of land for the descendants of Abraham extends across the generations of the ancestors. In addition to the three covenant promises in Gen 12, 15, 17, Yahweh’s oath to provide land for the descendants is recounted for Abraham (Gen 24:7), Isaac (Gen 26:3), Jacob (Gen 28:2–3), and Joseph (Gen 50:24). Additionally, it even serves as a motivating factor for Yahweh to respond to the Israelites in captivity in Egypt (Exod 2:24).

EXCURSUS: MICAH 7 AND ITS EXTENDED CONTEXT

These poetic images provide a powerful ending to Micah, but they do not end Micah’s role in the Book of the Twelve. When one reads Mic 7:8–20 in the context of the reign of Hezekiah, one encounters a dichotomy of the literary and the historical that is not easily resolved by reading Micah on its own.81 Literarily, whether reading Mic 7:8–20 against the backdrop of the siege of Sennacherib or reading the other accounts of this siege (2 Kgs 18–20; 2 Chr 32; Isa 36–39), one thing is clear: These literary accounts do not provide the full picture of the aftermath of the siege. To be sure, Jerusalem was spared, and Hezekiah remained on the throne, but the territory he controlled was greatly diminished.82 Hezekiah’s successor, Manasseh, ruled the country for fifty-five years with a very different political philosophy, one of accommodation to Assyrian hegemony, so that for much of the first three quarters of the seventh century BCE, there is little doubt that Judah functioned as a de facto vassal state to the Assyrian king. If read merely in isolation, the theological narratives and the hopeful conclusion to Micah leave a different impression. In the Book of the Twelve, however, Micah does not conclude the corpus. Rather, a series of connections invite the reader of the Twelve to see a close relationship between the sequence of Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah. Nahum celebrates the eventual downfall of Assyria in 612 BCE, but its opening theophanic hymn contains a number of catchwords back to Mic 7, and the core of the hymn provides a companion allusion to Exod 34:6–7 in Nah 1:3. Nahum’s allusion, however, focuses upon the message of 34:7 rather than 34:6. Exodus 34:7 affirms that while Yahweh’s compassion is long-suffering, Yahweh’s just character ultimately demands the punishment of the guilty. This idea opens Nah 1 before Nah 2–3 recounts Assyria’s punishment in graphic terms. The beginning of Habakkuk, however, complicates the story for Yahweh’s people. The situation at the beginning of Habakkuk (1:2–4) mirrors the same ethical problems that affected the country in Mic 6–7. In short, while the words of the people at the end of Mic 7 imply an expectation of changed behavior, nothing has changed when the focus shifts back to them in Hab 1:2–4. By the end of Habakkuk, the prophetic voice trembles (3:16) with the knowledge that punishment is indeed coming, this time from the Babylonians (Hab 1:5–12). Habakkuk 3:18 affirms that a remnant will survive, and even uses the language of Mic 7:7 to express this hopeful conviction: “I will wait for/exult in the God of my salvation.” The message of Zephaniah affirms that Jerusalem and Judah must be destroyed before a remnant can be gathered. The final promise of Zeph 3:19–20 reaches back to Mic 4:6–7 to establish the prediction and fulfilment motif for this remnant.83 In a very real sense, the message of Micah continues to play out in the Book of the Twelve.

16. Justice in this text means to act in harmony with Yahweh’s expectations for world order. See Johnson, “‏מִשׁפָט‎,” 86–98. The word derives from the root meaning “to judge” and has a wide range of meanings that can connote the action of justice/judgment, the place where the act is conducted, the result of the action, and the means by which the action is controlled. As such, different English words can be used: a legal statute, a verdict, justice, judgment, custom.

At Qumran, texts citing Mic 6:8 extend this same behavior to the realm of human-to-human interactions (see the citation in 1QS 4:5–6 and the allusion to Mic 6:8 in 1QS 8:2).

19. See Schart, Die Entstehung, 177–200. Schart lays out several points of contact, and his treatment of Mic 6:2–8 (191–97) includes connections to Mic 3:1, 8, 9; Hos 6:6; 12:6; as well as Amos 5:7, 24; 6:12. Schart concludes that Mic 6:8 is formulated to express the prophetic summation of Yahweh’s expectations for Hosea, Amos, and Micah. Werse evaluates 6:8 differently, arguing that the thematics of the verse reflect broad concerns found in too many Hebrew Bible texts to claim a redactional relationship elicited the formulation (Werse, Reconsidering the Book of the Four, 243–49). At the same time, Werse strengthens the arguments that the next unit of Mic 6:9–16 creates a more meaningful bridge to Zeph 1:1–2:3, which at the very least makes the placement of Mic 6:6–8 at this juncture in the book meaningful as a summary of Yahweh’s expectation and a transition to further accusations.

Oesch, Pericope 3 (Assen: Van Gorcum, 2000), 166–71. De Moor attempts to extend the prophetic speaker all the way to 7:13. See the rationale for rejecting these arguments in the discussion of 7:8 below.

36. The typical pattern of the complaint (German, Klage) includes a plea for divine action in some form. See Eberhard S. Gerstenberger, “Psalms,” in Hayes, Old Testament Form Criticism, 200.

37. While most recognize a relationship of some type, they express the type of relationship quite differently. Cf. Mays, 150; Rudolph, 123; Bo Reicke, “Liturgical Traditions in Micah 7,” HTR 60 (1967): 352, 354, 366; John T. Willis, “The Structure of the Book of Micah,” SEÅ 34 (1969): 29, 35–36; Jeremias, 213–14; Wolff, 203; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 177–80. E.g., Jeremias (213) makes the case that 7:1–7 relates closely to Mic 3:1–12 as an actualizing exposition of that chapter. Willis, by contrast, argues that these verses stem from the prophet himself. Wöhrle takes a different stance, associating the first-person singular style of the prophetic speaker in 7:1–7 with similar speeches in Mic 1–3. For him Mic 7:1–7 belongs to the early core of the Micah collection, predating the rest of the material in chs. 4–7.

38. Hermann Gunkel, “Der Micha-Schluss: Zur Einführung in die literaturgeschichtliche Arbeit am AT,” ZS 2 (1924): 145–78; Reicke, “Liturgical Traditions in Micah 7,” 349–67. Several others argue that a core composition was expanded so that 7:8–20 comes from more than one hand. Wolff (215), e.g., argues that only 7:11–13 comes from a later hand. By contrast, Wöhrle sees 7:8–20 as the result of five redactional layers (Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 180–88; see also his summary chart, 197). These suggestions problematically assume too quickly that the variations in expression require separate compositional hands. The approach taken here treats the changes in speaker as responses to the preceding issues, without imposing such fine theological distinctions in this instance.

39. See discussion in Jeremias, 215; Wolff, 203; Mays, 151; Rudolph, 123.

40. See Wolff, 204–5.

43. See Kessler, 287–90.

44. A number of commentators have suggested that 7:4b, or portions thereof, represents a later, isolated gloss, because it changes topics so abruptly from the preceding. See Wolff, 202; Jeremias, 216.

45. The day of Yahweh is a recurring theme in the Book of the Twelve, and it can be elicited without specifying the name Yahweh. See Rolf Rendtorff, “How to Read the Book of the Twelve as a Theological Unity,” in Nogalski and Sweeney, Reading and Hearing the Book of the Twelve, 75–87; and Nogalski, “The Day(s) of YHWH,” 192–213; Nogalski, “Recurring Themes in the Book of the Twelve,” 125–36.

47. James D. Nogalski, “Micah 7:8–20,” in The Bible as a Human Witness to Divine Revelation: Hearing the Word of God through Historically Dissimilar Traditions, ed. Randall Heskett and Brian P. Irwin, LHBOTS 469 (New York: T&T Clark, 2010), 125–42.

48. Of course, reference to Hezekiah’s payment comes closer to the beginning of the Kings account than to the end of the story, which leaves open the possibility of when such payment was made. Nevertheless, assuming that Hezekiah did pay tribute to Sennacherib, it also makes sense that this payment would not have been publicly acknowledged by Hezekiah, so that if the payment was indeed made to procure Sennacherib’s departure, to the majority of the population the retreat of the Assyrian army would have indeed seemed miraculous. See the discussion in Miller and Hayes, History of Israel and Judah, 400–403; and Albertz, History of Israelite Religion, 162.

49. The precise phrase ʾlōhê yišʿî elsewhere appears only in Pss 18:46; 25:5; 27:9 (see also the similar phrases in 51:14 and 81:1).

50. For a more thorough treatment of the narrative arc running from the end of Micah through Habakkuk, see James D. Nogalski, “One Book and Twelve Books: The Nature of the Redactional Work and the Implications of Cultic Source Material in the Book of the Twelve,” in Ben Zvi, Nogalski, and Römer, Two Sides of the Coin, 30–39.

51. Gunkel, “Der Micha-Schluss,” 145–78. See also Reicke, “Liturgical Traditions in Micah 7,” 349–67.

52. Nogalski, “Micah 7:8–20,” 125–42; Sweeney, 2:408–9. In a different way, Jeremias (219, 221) treats 7:8–20 with regard to the book of Micah’s thematic blocks but sees the audience as the postexilic community. Regardless of whether one considers 7:8–20 to have been compiled for the end of Micah originally, or whether one believes an independent liturgy was simply placed at the end of the book, one almost certainly has to conclude that the enemy in 7:8–10 should be interpreted as Assyria (or more specifically, Lady Nineveh). If 7:8–20 existed prior to being attached to Micah, the editor who appended it likely considered it appropriate to conclude the collection named for Micah, a prophet at the end of the eighth century.

53. De Moor, “Micah 7:1–13,” 149–96.

54. De Moor attempts to read 7:8–13 as a continuation of the prophetic speaker (de Moor, “Micah 7:1–13,” 167–69). He is followed by Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 181–82. The majority of his evidence hinges upon treating instances of reception history as evidence for a primary reading. He finds more than thirty medieval manuscripts that interpret the feminine singular suffix in 7:10 as masculine singular. Naturally, in unpointed texts, the two would look identical, and one could treat the changing speakers more simply if the pronoun was masculine rather than feminine. The problem comes when trying to explain how the feminine pointing would have arisen. He essentially assigns the change to a first-century CE misogynistic interpreter who considered it better to change the prophet’s gender here than to have the prophet speak a prediction that did not come to pass. Such reasoning is difficult to comprehend. More likely, the more difficult feminine pointing represents the original reading.

55. One must infer the identity of the woman speaking to her enemy from the context and from the constellation of available speakers in prophetic texts in general. The next subunit (7:11–13) addresses the woman who speaks in 7:8–10, meaning the speaker has changed beginning with 7:11. The use of various motifs in 7:11 (esp. the building of your [second-person feminine singular] walls) make clear contextually that the woman being addressed is Jerusalem personified, or Lady Zion (see the treatment of Lady Zion in the commentary to Mic 4:8–13).

58. See esp. Fitzgerald, “Mythological Background,” 403–16. Fitzgerald demonstrates how this imagery conveys royal connotations as the queen who is responsible for her city.

67. Wolff, 224–25; Jeremias, 225–26; Mays, 162; Rudolph, 132–33. By way of contrast, see Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 131–33. Wöhrle correctly sees the phrase as an enemy attack, but he thinks that the second-person feminine singular suffixes in 7:11–12 are directed against the enemy addressed in 7:8–10.

68. See Judg 9:52. Note also that Samson “comes to” Lehi and then proceeds to kill one thousand Philistines (Judg 15:14).

69. See Wolff, 225; Mays; Jeremias, 131. If it does represent an isolated gloss, it suggests that someone read 7:12 as a threat rather than a promise.

70. Wolff (225) sees the verse as a juxtaposition, inserted to expand the enemy in 7:8, 10, perhaps in light of Isa 24:1–6. Andersen and Freedman (588) treat the verse as “transitional” and an “interlude.” They recognize, however, that the verse “does not seem to fit either the triumphal tone of vv 11–12 or the reconstructive tone of vv 14–17.” It is not clear, however, how 7:13 functions as a transition when it lacks a clear connection to that which precedes or follows it. See Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 181–86; and Utzschneider, 165. Wöhrle correctly interprets 7:11–13 as a threat from the foreign nations, though his insistence on assigning 7:10b–13 to a separate redactional layer (one of five in this passage) rather than the surrounding verses is not convincing. Utzschneider also argues that 7:13 refers to the enemy in 7:8–10, and that this statement is not about universal destruction but actually fits with the general theme of Micah, as evidenced by the condemnation of Samaria (1:7) and the city (6:13) with similar language.

73. See discussion in text note.

74. The fear of the nations motif plays a recurring role in the story of the lead-up to the entry into the land. See Exod 9:30; Num 22:3; Deut 2:25; 3:2, 22; 31:6; Josh 2:9, 24; 4:24.

75. See Nogalski, Books of Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah, 122–24, 178, 380–84. Read the commentary to Joel 2:13; 4:21; and Jonah 4:2 regarding the importance of Exod 34:6–7 for the Book of the Twelve.

76. According to Wolff (216–17), Bernhard Stade, Wilhelm Nowack, and Karl Marti represent classic examples from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries of those isolating multiple sources, as they separate the stylistic changes of the second- and third-person references to Yahweh. Wolff (217) himself agrees with those who believe that such vacillation typifies liturgical forms.

77. See Wolff, 230–31; Rudolph, 135–36.

78. Ironically, both Wolff (230) and Rudolph (135) consider 7:19 the most original portion of the hymn, since traditional idioms comprise most of 7:18–19. Others have noted that the language of Mic 7:19b and Jonah 2:3(4) are quite similar to one another, which could explain 7:19b as an insertion. See Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 153; Nogalski, Book of the Twelve, 592. See also Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 187–88, 196–97. He sees the entire hymnic conclusion (7:18–20) as a later addition associated with his so-called grace layer (see the introduction to the Book of the Twelve in this commentary).

79. The linking of adjacent writings in the Book of the Twelve through the use of citations is not unique. A similar phenomenon occurs between Joel and Amos, where Joel 4:16 cites Amos 1:2 and Joel 4:18 cites Amos 9:13. These two citations mean that Joel 4:16–18 essentially alludes to the beginning and end of Amos (1:2; 9:13). Genetically, Amos 9:13 was probably added to cement the link back to Joel 4:18 because the Joel language in Amos 9:13 is literarily suspect compared to its context (Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 116–21).

80. See Jeremias, 230.

82. Miller and Hayes, History of Israel and Judah, 410–21.

83. See Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 209–11; Nogalski, Book of the Twelve, 519, 558, 703–4.
